‘We review a preliminary injunction for abuse of discretion.” A 
preliminary injunction should issue only if the states, as movants, estabhsh
(1) a substantial likelihood of success on the merits, (2) a 
substantial threat of irreparable injury if the injunction is not 
issued, (3) that the threatened injury if the injunction is denied 
outweighs any harm that will result if the injunction is granted, 
and (4) that the grant of an injunction will not disserve the public 
interest.
“As to each element of the district court’s pre!im in a ry-i njim ction

* * * now] address whether Texas has established a substantial 
likelihood of success on its claim that DAPA must be submitted for notice 
and comment. * * *
The government advances the notion that DAPA is exempt from notice 
and comment as a policy statement. We evaluate two criteria to distinguish 
policy statements from substantive rules: whether the rule (1) “impose[s] 
any rights and obligations” and (2) “genuinely leaves the agency and its 
decision-makers free to exercise discretion.” [Professionals and Patients for 
Customized Care v. Shalala, 56 F.3d 592, 595 (5th Cir.1995) (quoting 
Community Nutrition Institute v. Young, 818 F.2d 943, 946 (D.C. Cir. 
1987).] There is some overlap in the analysis of those prongs “because ‘[i]f 
a statement denies the decisionmaker discretion in the area of its coverage 
. . . then the statement is binding, and creates rights or obligations.’ ” 
[General Electric v. EPA, 290 F.3d 377, 382 (D.C. Cir. 2002).] “Whfie 
mindful but suspicious of the agency’s own characterization, we . . . focus [ ] 
primarily on whether the rule has binding effect on agency discretion or 
severely restricts it.” [Professionals and Patients, 56 F.3d at 595.] “[A]n 
agency pronouncement will be considered binding as a practical matter if 
it either appears on its face to be binding, or is applied by the agency in a 
way that indicates it is binding.” General Electric, 290 F.3d at 383 (citation 
omitted).
Although the DAPA Memo facially purports to confer discretion, the 
district court determined that “[n]othing about DAPA 'genuinely leaves the 
agency and its [employees] 6*00 to exercise discretion,’ ” a factual finding 
that we review for clear error. That finding was partly informed by analysis 
of the implementation of DACA, the precursor to DAPA.
